meta: Time: 3 hours · Maximum marks: 100 · Modelled on the April 2026 NIOS paper (new syllabus)
instructions: The question paper consists of 27 questions. All questions are compulsory; where there is an OR, answer one.
Questions 1–13 are objective (MCQ, True/False, match, fill in the blanks, one word) of 1 mark per part.
Questions 14–19 carry 2 marks (30–40 words). Question 21 has five parts of 2 marks. Questions 20 and 27 carry 3 marks, 22 and 24–26 carry 4 marks, and 23 carries 6 marks (150–200 words).
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

questions.q: According to the passage, drug addiction is —
Which of these is NOT a behavioural therapy mentioned?
Which word in the passage means 'a systematic plan or set of rules'?
The ultimate goal of drug abuse treatment is —
Short-term treatment methods last —

sections.passage: Drug addiction is a treatable disorder. Through treatment that is tailored to individual needs, patients can leave their condition and live normal, productive lives. Like people with diabetes or heart disease, people in treatment for addiction learn behavioural changes and often take medications as part of their treatment regimen. Behavioural therapies can include counselling, psychotherapy, support groups, or family therapy. Treatment offers help in suppressing the withdrawal syndrome and drug craving and in blocking the effects of drugs. In general, the more treatment given, the better the results. Patients who stay in treatment longer have better outcomes than those who stay less time. Studies have shown that treatment works to reduce drug use and crimes committed by drug-dependent people. The ultimate goal of all drug abuse treatment is to enable the patient to achieve lasting abstinence, but the immediate goals are to reduce drug use, improve the patient's ability to function, and minimise the medical and social curse of drug abuse. Short-term methods last less than six months and include residential therapy, medication therapy, and drug-free outpatient therapy. Longer-term treatment may include, for example, methadone maintenance outpatient treatment for opiate addicts and residential therapeutic communities.

sections.passage:
For centuries, honeybees have quietly done one of the most important jobs on our planet. As they move from flower to flower collecting nectar, they carry pollen that allows plants to produce fruits and seeds. Nearly one-third of the food we eat — apples, almonds, mustard, coffee and many vegetables — depends on such pollination.

Yet bee populations are declining in many parts of the world. Farmers spray pesticides that kill bees along with pests. Forests and wild flowering plants are cleared for buildings and single-crop farms, leaving bees with little variety of food. Climate change has made flowers bloom earlier or later than usual, so bees and blossoms no longer meet at the right time.

The good news is that ordinary people can help. Planting native flowering plants, avoiding chemical sprays in gardens and buying honey from local beekeepers all support bees. Some cities now keep beehives on rooftops. Protecting these tiny workers is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of our own survival.

sections.passage: The Indian postal service is one of the largest in the world, with more than 1.5 lakh post offices, most of them in villages. Long before mobile phones, the postman was a familiar figure who carried letters, money orders and news of joy and sorrow. Today, India Post has changed with the times. It runs savings banks and insurance schemes, delivers parcels for online shopping companies and offers banking at the doorstep through the India Post Payments Bank. A floating post office on Dal Lake in Srinagar and one of the world's highest post offices at Hikkim in Himachal Pradesh show how far the service reaches.

questions.q: Why did the bearded man ask the king's forgiveness? (Three Questions)
questions.answer: He had come to kill the king, but the king had saved his life instead. Grateful and ashamed, he begged forgiveness and promised that he and his sons would serve the king faithfully.

or.q: How did the hermit prove that the king had already received his answers? (Three Questions)

questions.q: Describe the setting of the story. (After Twenty Years)

questions.q: What did the Loisels do to find the necklace? (The Necklace)
questions.answer: They searched the folds of her dress and cloak. Loisel retraced their route on foot and went to the police, the cab companies and the newspapers, offering a reward, but found nothing.

or.q: How did the Loisels' life change after they bought the new necklace? (The Necklace)
or.answer: They dismissed the servant and moved to a garret. Mathilde did the heavy housework and haggled for every sou, while Loisel worked extra jobs. In ten years Mathilde became old, coarse and rough.

questions.q: Why does Bacon compare natural abilities to natural plants? (Of Studies)
questions.answer: Just as plants need pruning to grow well, our natural talents need to be trimmed and shaped by study. Study improves raw abilities, and experience in turn corrects study.

questions.q: What is the turning point in 'The Necklace'? How does it change Mathilde? (The Necklace)
questions.answer: The loss of the necklace is the turning point. It forces Mathilde from dreams of luxury into ten years of poverty and toil. She becomes hard-working, brave and honest about her debt, though she loses her beauty and youth.

or.q: Why is the ending of 'An Astrologer's Day' a surprise? How does Narayan prepare for it? (An Astrologer's Day)
or.answer: We learn only at the end that the astrologer himself had stabbed Guru Nayak, which explains his fear, his knowledge and his advice. Narayan prepares for it with hints: the astrologer left his village suddenly, he feels uneasy when he sees the stranger's face, and he tries to return the anna and leave.

sections.passage:
When Arjun's village school got its first computer lab, nobody knew how to use it. The machines sat under plastic covers for months, because the only teacher who understood computers had been transferred. Arjun, a Class XI student, could not bear to see them unused. He had learnt the basics on his uncle's laptop during the holidays.

With the headmaster's permission, he began staying back after school to teach younger children how to type, draw and search for information. At first only five students came. Within a month the number grew to forty, and some parents joined too, wanting to learn how to check crop prices and apply for government schemes online.

Arjun soon realised that he too had much to learn. He watched free online courses at night and wrote down every question the children asked. When the district officer visited the school, she was surprised to see grandmothers sending e-mails. She arranged for a trained teacher and an internet connection, and asked Arjun to help train other village volunteers. 'I only wanted the computers to be used,' Arjun said shyly. 'I did not know that teaching would teach me so much.'

questions.q: Write a paragraph (150–200 words) on 'The Role of Youth in Keeping Our Surroundings Clean'.
questions.answer:
The Role of Youth in Keeping Our Surroundings Clean
Clean surroundings are the foundation of good health and a pleasant life, and young people can play a leading role in keeping them so. Youth have energy, ideas and the ability to influence others, especially on social media. They can begin at home by segregating wet and dry waste, composting kitchen waste and refusing single-use plastic. In schools and colleges they can run cleanliness drives, maintain eco-clubs and put up dustbins and posters. In their neighbourhoods they can organise weekend clean-ups of parks, lanes and water bodies, and persuade shopkeepers to use cloth or paper bags. By making short videos and street plays, they can spread awareness about the dangers of littering and open burning of garbage. Most important, young people must set an example: they should never throw waste on the roads or spit in public places. When the youth lead by example, others follow, and the dream of a clean and healthy India comes closer to reality.

or.q: Write a summary of the passage above (on the return of millets) in about 60 words.
or.answer: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi, once India's staple food, were pushed aside by rice and wheat after the Green Revolution but are now returning. They are highly nutritious and good for diabetics, and they grow in dry, hot areas with little water and fertiliser. The UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, and schemes and start-ups are promoting them.

sections.passage: The millets — jowar, bajra, ragi and others — were once the staple food of India. After the Green Revolution, rice and wheat took their place, and millets came to be seen as poor people's food. Today they are making a comeback. Millets are rich in fibre, iron, calcium and protein, have a low glycaemic index and are good for people with diabetes. They are also good for the planet: they grow in dry areas, need little water and few fertilisers, and can survive high temperatures, which makes them suitable in a time of climate change. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion. To popularise them, the government is including millets in mid-day meals, and many start-ups now sell millet biscuits, noodles and snacks.

questions.answer:

From: Safety Officer
Date: 15 February 2026
Subject: Fire in the staff room on 14 February 2026

2. Cause: an overheated microwave oven with a faulty cord.
